title: Khalsa College, 1892
hook: a Sikh college rises in Amritsar

segments.voice: Yesterday, Professor Gurmukh Singh, and your line was the teacher. What did you teach, and to whom? Today, the college he argued for. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

Outside Amritsar, on open ground along the road toward Lahore, a crowd gathers for a foundation stone. British officials in formal dress. Supporters from the Sikh princely states. Singh Sabha reformers, teachers and writers. And ordinary Sikhs who've given what they could, so that this could happen. Nothing stands there yet but a stone and a plan. The plan is a college where young Sikhs can learn science and English without being taught to leave their Gurus behind. Today: Khalsa College.
screen: `A FOUNDATION STONE.` → `PRINCES, REFORMERS, ORDINARY GIVERS.` → `A COLLEGE NOT YET BUILT.`

segments.voice: First, why a college. The Singh Sabha reformers had schools and papers. But young Sikhs who wanted higher study went to colleges run by the government or by missions, and some, as the reformers saw it, came back strangers to their own tradition. The reformers wanted a place that taught the modern subjects and Sikh learning under one roof. Second, who paid. Sikh rulers of the princely states gave large sums. The British government gave its support. And collections went around the Punjab, in towns and villages, from people with little to spare. The college belonged, in that sense, to everyone who put something in. Third, the name. Khalsa is the name Guru Gobind Singh gave the community of the initiated, those who belong directly to the Guru. A Khalsa College says what it's for in its name: a college for that community, open to learning from anywhere, rooted in the Guru's word. Over time, a great building rose on that ground, and generations of students passed through it. Fourth, what the Gurus say about learning. In a hymn in Asa, Guru Nanak says that when learning is truly reflected on, the learned one becomes a help to others. Learning that stays in the head, or serves only pride, misses the point. The founders hoped the college would turn out graduates who served: teachers, doctors, writers and leaders who carried what they'd learned back into the Panth. A college is, in the end, a promise that learning will be passed on. Every time you learn something new and share it, you keep a small version of that promise.
screen: `WHY A SIKH COLLEGE.` · `PRINCES, OFFICIALS, ORDINARY GIVERS.` · `KHALSA — THE GURU'S OWN.` · `LEARNING THAT HELPS OTHERS.` · then, large: `A COLLEGE FOR THE KHALSA.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for something new. Sit, and breathe slowly. Choose one small thing you'd like to learn this week: a word of Punjabi, a line of a hymn, how a plant grows, the name of a street you walk down. Hold it in mind as a question. Breathe in, curious. Breathe out, patient. Then ask one more thing: who could this help, once I know it? Let that person come to mind. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru between the breaths. The bell holds the time.
Khalsa College. The Sikh college founded in Amritsar to teach modern subjects alongside the Gurus' learning, built with gifts from princes and ordinary Sikhs. Today's word.
Your line: a college for the khalsa. Today, learn one new thing, and pass it on to one person before you sleep. Day nine hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Khalsa College in Amritsar as a fruit of the Singh Sabha reform, built with gifts from Sikh princes and ordinary Sikhs, and it still teaches students today.

notes: The foundation stone was laid by the Lieutenant-Governor of the Punjab (Sir James Lyall); the voice says only 'British officials'. Confirm before naming.
Funding from Sikh princely states, government support and public collections: confirm framing; no sums are given under the claims rule.
'On open ground along the road toward Lahore': confirm the site description.
The Persian khalisa (crown land) etymology for Khalsa was cut from the trapdoor under the claims rule; a Keeper may restore it from the encyclopedia entry.
Ang 356 (Asa M1, 'vidya veechari ta(n) parupkari') paraphrased; confirm the Ang.
Editor: cut the Persian khalisa etymology from the trapdoor (claims rule) and the invented 'a coin, a week's wages' detail in the hook.

Auditor: 'Sikh princes' present at the stone-laying is unverified, softened to 'supporters from the Sikh princely states'; the 'strangers to their own tradition' claim about mission and government colleges is now the reformers' view, not the narrator's; dropped the repeated 'Why it matters' formula.
